questions.prompt: A pure delay of \(T_d\) seconds has the transfer function
questions.explanation: The delay shifts the signal and does not change its size, so the magnitude is 1 and the phase is \(-\omega T_d\) radians. A real pole would change the magnitude. The growing exponential is the advance, not the delay. A sample period is a discrete-time quantity and is not this transfer function.

questions.prompt: A delay of \(0.04\) seconds is read at \(10\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The phase lag, as a positive number of degrees, is
questions.explanation: The phase is \(-\omega T_d\) radians. The lag is \(0.04 \cdot 10 = 0.4\) radians, which is \(0.4 \cdot 180/\pi = 22.9183\) degrees. Reporting 0.4 as degrees skips the conversion. Reporting \(\omega T_d\) in radians is the right angle only when the unit asked for is radians.

questions.prompt: The first-order Padé model of a \(0.25\) second delay has its pole at
questions.explanation: The model is \((1 - s T_d/2)/(1 + s T_d/2)\). The pole is at \(-2/T_d = -2/0.25 = -8\). The zero is the mirror, at \(+8\), in the right half-plane. The delay itself, 0.25, is not a pole.

questions.prompt: Write the phase, in radians, of \(e^{-s T_d}\) at frequency \(w\), in the names w and td. \(T_d\) is the name td.
questions.explanation: On \(s = jw\) the exponent is \(-jw\cdot td\), so the phase is \(-w\cdot td\) radians. The positive product \(w\cdot td\) is the lag, not the signed phase. Dividing by \(w\) returns the delay, which is not an angle.

questions.prompt: A loop has a phase margin of \(50^\circ\) at a crossover of \(8\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The delay margin, in seconds, is
questions.explanation: Convert the margin to radians before dividing by the crossover. \(50 \cdot \pi/180\) radians, divided by 8, is 0.109083 seconds. Dividing the degree number by the crossover, \(50/8 = 6.25\), treats degrees as radians and overstates the delay the loop can tolerate.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use to check how much delay a loop can take.
questions.explanation: The margin and the crossover are the two measurements. Degrees have to become radians because the delay formula multiplies \(\omega\) by seconds and gets radians. Dividing then converts that angle into a time. The last step is what the number means. Dividing degrees by the crossover skips the conversion and quotes a time that is too long by \(180/\pi\).

questions.prompt: A calculation treats a delay of \(0.2\) seconds at \(5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: \(\omega T_d = 5 \cdot 0.2 = 1\) radian, not 1 degree. The phase is \(-1\) radian, about \(-57.3\) degrees. The transfer function and the unit magnitude are right, and the Padé model does have a right-half-plane zero.

steps: The transfer function of the delay is \(e^{-s T_d}\).
Its magnitude at every finite frequency is 1.
At this frequency the phase is \(-1\) degree.
A first-order Padé model of the same delay has a right-half-plane zero and a left-half-plane pole.

The Padé model has a left-half-plane zero, so the last step is the flawed one.

questions.prompt: Compared with the pure delay, the first-order Padé model
questions.explanation: The first-order model is an all-pass: magnitude 1 everywhere, like the delay. Its phase matches \(-\omega T_d\) for small \(\omega T_d\) and then levels off, while the pure delay's lag grows without bound. A right-half-plane zero does not make the model itself unstable. The pole is in the left half-plane. A sample period is a different object.

matches the magnitude of 1 at every frequency, and matches the phase only near \(\omega = 0\)
is unstable, because it has a right-half-plane zero

questions.prompt: Which statements about a pure delay \(e^{-s T_d}\) are true?
questions.explanation: The magnitude is identically 1, and the phase \(-\omega T_d\) runs to \(-\infty\) as \(\omega\) grows. The delay is not a rational pole. The first-order Padé replacement does have a zero at \(+2/T_d\).

questions.prompt: At \(20\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), a delay of \(0.15\) seconds has magnitude
questions.explanation: \(e^{-j\omega T_d}\) lies on the unit circle, so the magnitude is 1 at every frequency, including \(20\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The phase lag \(20 \cdot 0.15 = 3\) radians is an angle, not a magnitude. A magnitude of \(e^{-3}\) would be right for a real exponential, not for a pure phase shift.

questions.prompt: Extra delay in a loop that was already near \(-180^\circ\) at crossover
questions.explanation: Phase falls by \(\omega T_d\) radians. At crossover that subtraction comes straight out of the phase margin, and the magnitude being 1 does not put the phase back. The shift is a loss, not a raise. A delay does not cancel a right-half-plane zero.

questions.prompt: A delay makes a robust-stability disk harder to certify because
questions.explanation: Delay spends phase and can force \(|T|\) to stay large near the new, fragile crossover. The weight then has less room under the small-gain bound. Delay does not make the low-frequency complementary sensitivity grow without bound, it is not automatically an unstable nominal loop, and it is not a pole at \(-1/T_d\).
